summary: Deep dive on p95/p99 tail latency for Lyra's conversational assistant. Focused on streaming vs non-streaming behavior, KV cache hit patterns, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact, and additional network hops for VPC/on-prem. Identified likely tail causes: cold KV cache misses, batching-induced queuing under bursty traffic, and occasional kernel hot-path regressions on long sequences. Agreed next steps include KV stress testing, sharing profiling artifacts, and planning a small dedicated pilot to reproduce tail under controlled conditions.
topics: KV cache behavior and eviction effects
quantization effects on throughput and variability
network hops, TLS, and VPC/on-prem latency additions
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on this account. We're joined by Priya (SE). Agenda: walk through your p95/p99 numbers, streaming vs non-streaming differences, KV cache, batching, quant, and VPC hops.
[00:23] Samir Rao: Great, thanks. Quick backfill — Lyra runs a customer-facing assistant, about 120 requests/s average, spikes to 700 qps during peak, seq length median ~128 tokens but tail to 1024 for long context. We see p95 around 220ms for short replies but p99 spikes up to 1.2s which is hurting UX.
[00:50] Priya Shah: thanks Samir. Couple clarifying q's: is 120 rps sustained or aggregated across regions? and are you streaming tokens to users or waiting for full response?
[01:05] Maria Gomez: it's aggregated; majority in us-east. We currently do non-streaming end-to-end for safety checks and post-processing, so users see full response after generation finishes.
[01:20] Alex Kim: that already explains some of the perceived latency; streaming can drastically reduce time-to-first-token though it doesn't change total compute. But p99 being 1.2s suggests tail causes beyond just CPU, likely cache misses or queuing.
[01:40] Ethan Wu: we run on GCP with a VPC peering to our infra, TLS termination at our edge, then calls into Redwood hosted region. Could be extra network hops there, also we're on 10Gb links.
[01:55] Priya Shah: ok noted. To frame the rest — we'll cover 1) measurement (how you're computing p95/p99), 2) runtime sources of tail, 3) mitigations (kv, batching, quant, routing).
[02:10] Samir Rao: quick note on measurement — we sample at the edge, so the time includes network hops into Redwood and back, plus our internal checks. We can share raw histograms.
[02:25] Priya Shah: perfect. On measurement: make sure you're computing server-side p95/p99 (ex token generation) and client-side. We often see client p99 much higher because of retries, network jitter, and TLS renegotiation. Also check if you include first byte vs last byte.
[02:50] Maria Gomez: we compute total round trip from request to receipt of final payload.
[02:58] Priya Shah: ok that includes network. For server-side, our internal metric for p95/p99 on token-generation (non-streaming) under similar load tends to be lower — p95 ~180ms, p99 ~420ms on dedicated configs for short contexts.
[03:20] Alex Kim: let's talk streaming vs non-streaming. Streaming sends tokens as they're ready. For a 200-token reply with a 20ms/token avg, non-streaming waits ~4s then returns; streaming gives first token in ~150-250ms and subsequent tokens incrementally. Streaming reduces perceived latency and the p99 for time-to-first-token, but if you have batching, streaming can complicate things because we need to flush partial results while respecting batch windows.
[03:50] Maria Gomez: interesting — so streaming would give better UX even if compute time similar. But our safety pipeline currently requires full output for QA. Any suggestions?
[03:58] Priya Shah: common approach: stream while doing a lightweight safety filter inline, then re-score full output downstream asynchronously. Another pattern is to stream with a holdback buffer for the first N tokens while you run quick checks. Depends on risk tolerance.
[04:20] Ethan Wu: back to p99 spikes - in our traces we saw large outliers aligned with cold KV cache misses — some requests that hit new prefixes were substantially slower. Can you explain the KV cache interaction?
[04:35] Priya Shah: sure — KV cache (the attention key/value cache) is used to avoid recomputing prefix tokens. On Redwood runtime we keep per-session KV cached in memory; cache hits mean generating only new tokens. Misses require re-encoding prefix (or retransferring KV), which can add multiples of base latency depending on prefix length and how we materialize cache. Also eviction during memory pressure causes transient p99 spikes.
[04:58] Samir Rao: eviction — are you saying our long sessions might evict older sessions and cause rebuilds?
[05:05] Priya Shah: exactly. If you have a lot of long-running contexts and limited KV memory, eviction/reload across processes or nodes creates a jank. We can mitigate with sticky routing to keep sessions on same shards, increase KV memory, or use persistent KV stores for very long-lived sessions (tradeoff: network IO).
[05:25] Alex Kim: another common tail cause is batching and queuing. If you set batch windows to maximize throughput, a single slow-request inside a batch or batching during spikes can increase latency for all requests in that batch — it amplifies tail.
[05:40] Maria Gomez: what's typical batching strategy? We thought bigger batches always lower cost.
[05:45] Priya Shah: bigger batches increase throughput and lower per-token CPU cost, but they increase per-request latency due to the batch wait window. For bursty workloads or when you care about p99, smaller or adaptive batching helps. Redwood supports dynamic batching where we auto-shrink batch windows under latency pressure. For p99-sensitive services we often recommend pinned minimal batch size or CPU/GPU reservations to avoid queuing.
[06:10] Ethan Wu: any numbers to illustrate?
[06:13] Priya Shah: rough example: without batching, token latency might be 18ms; with a batch of 8 you could be at 18ms compute + a 40-120ms batching wait depending on arrival rate — that wait dominates tail if arrival is bursty. Under low QPS, batching waits longer to fill the batch.
[06:32] Alex Kim: quantization note — using int8/4 quant can speed up compute and reduce p99 by reducing kernel time, but quant introduces compatibility issues for some ops and sometimes changes memory layout triggering different kernel paths. So test end-to-end; we have verified profiles for common open models but custom models need validation.
[06:52] Maria Gomez: we're using a tuned 7B variant; we've tried fp16, thinking about int8. How big an effect on p99 should we expect?
[06:58] Priya Shah: on many GPUs int8 can reduce per-token compute by ~20-40% which reduces contribution to tail. But if quant causes more memory pressure (due to packing) or forces fallback kernels, you might see unexpected p99 increases. We'll run kernel-selection profiling for your model.
[07:20] Samir Rao: you mentioned kernel selection and compilation — can you say more about the hot-path regressions? We've seen occasional 300ms blips without obvious upstream causes.
[07:30] Priya Shah: some layers or sequence lengths choose different CUDA kernels or fallbacks in cuBLAS/cuDNN etc. If the runtime switches kernels mid-run (e.g., due to sequence length crossing a threshold or a new code path being JIT-compiled), the first few requests that hit that path pay compile/setup cost which shows up as a spike. We mitigate by pre-warming common sequence lengths and ensuring binary kernels are cached.
[07:55] Alex Kim: also consider model variants: if your routing sometimes falls back to a cheaper quantized variant on capacity pressure, that fallback can change latency profile and quality. We log model variant changes and can set routing policies to avoid unexpected fallbacks during critical windows.
[08:12] Ethan Wu: about network hops — we have TLS termination at our edge and then a hop to Redwood. How many extra ms should we budget?
[08:18] Priya Shah: each extra hop adds RTT; within the same region a well-provisioned VPC peering might add 5-30ms. Cross-region or private MPLS can add 50-200ms. Also TLS handshake and small MTU fragmentation can add jitter. We recommend mutual TLS with session reuse and keep-alive to avoid handshake overhead; also colocating Redwood dedicated endpoints inside your VPC (private deployment) removes internet egress variability.
[08:48] Maria Gomez: if we move to a private deployment on our VPC, does that remove all tail sources?
[08:55] Priya Shah: it removes a class of network variability and noisy neighbors in shared hosting, but tail can still come from KV evictions, batching queuing, kernel hot paths, or GC/OS scheduling on the host. Private reduces network-induced jitter and gives you control to tune instance types and NUMA.
[09:12] Samir Rao: ok that helps. For our cases where long contexts are frequent, what immediate mitigations do you recommend?
[09:18] Priya Shah: quick list: 1) instrument and separate server-side token-gen p95/p99 from client-side. 2) enable sticky session routing for long-lived dialogs to keep KV warm. 3) reduce batch windows or use adaptive batching for latency-sensitive routes. 4) test int8 in a canary to measure p99 impact. 5) pre-warm kernels for your common seq lengths.
[09:40] Alex Kim: plus consider a small dedicated pilot (2-4 nodes) so we can reproduce spikes with identical hardware and disable noisy neighbor effects. We'll provide a runbook for running controlled spike tests.
[09:52] Maria Gomez: is there tooling to show per-request breakdown (queue, kernel, network)?
[09:58] Priya Shah: yes — Redwood traces include per-token timing breakdown: queue_wait, kv_lookup_ms, kernel_ms, serialization, and network. We'll share an example trace and a spreadsheet mapping fields.
[10:12] Alex Kim: I'll share the benchmark_spreadsheet.xlsx (link in chat) and the p99_runbook.
[10:18] Ethan Wu: regarding KV persistence — you mentioned persistent KV stores as an option; network IO there could add latency right?
[10:24] Priya Shah: yes persistent KV avoids in-memory eviction but introduces network fetch latency on cold reads. For very long sessions it's often better because hot sessions stay in memory and cold ones pay the fetch. The key is to ensure the KV store is low-latency (co-located SSD/NVMe) or use a local RAM-backed LRU + async persistent backing. We'll discuss architecture options in docs.
[10:44] Maria Gomez: what about query routing — can you route traffic during spikes to cheaper models? We worry about QOS if quality drops.
[10:50] Alex Kim: Redwood supports routing rules to prefer low-latency variants or fall back to cheaper ones under capacity pressure; you can set per-route quality SLAs so critical routes never downgrade. That helps control cost without surprising production routes.
[11:06] Samir Rao: any examples where switching to streaming actually increased p99 for entire session?
[11:12] Priya Shah: yes if you implement blocking safety checks that wait for full token sequence server-side before letting tokens flow, you might add an extra safety-induced latency. Also streaming with aggressive batching that waits to flush chunks can make time-to-first-token worse if chunk-size and batch windows are misaligned. The implementation details matter.
[11:30] Maria Gomez: ok actionable items — can you run a KV stress and a kernel-profile against our model?
[11:36] Priya Shah: yes — we'll run a 1-hour KV stress with simulated long sessions and provide flamegraphs. We'll also run kernel selection profiling for your model under sequences of 128, 256, 512, 1024.
[11:50] Ethan Wu: we'll provide seq distributions and sample payloads.
[11:55] Alex Kim: perfect. I'll send a pilot plan and pricing. Any final questions?
[12:02] Maria Gomez: one last — do you have guidance on preferred batch/window settings for a mixed workload?
[12:08] Priya Shah: for mixed workloads we recommend adaptive batching with per-route latency SLOs — set a 99th latency target and the runtime tunes batch size dynamically; if you need manual settings, aim for batch size 2-4 with a max window of 20-40ms for latency-sensitive routes. For high-throughput offline routes, use bigger batches.
[12:28] Samir Rao: sounds good. Thanks all.
[12:32] Alex Kim: thanks everyone — recap and next steps in chat. I'll upload runbook and the spreadsheet. Priya will run the tests. Ethan will upload histograms.
[12:45] Maria Gomez: thank you.

Notes/links: benchmark_spreadsheet.xlsx (shared in chat), p99_runbook.md (will be sent), kv_stress_test_script.sh (SE to run), profiling-flamegraphs link TBD.
